summary: Updates the URN namespace for National Bibliography Numbers, identifiers national libraries use for resources not covered by standard identifier systems such as ISBN. It revises the namespace that was established in 2001.

eli5.summary: Libraries give a number to each item that has no ISBN. This lets those numbers be written like web names so computers can find them.

questions: what is a national bibliography number
how is a urn nbn resolved
what does urn nbn syntax look like
subtitle: How national library identifiers are written as persistent, globally unique URNs, with the namespace brought up to date.

tldr.problem: National libraries assign National Bibliography Numbers to resources that standard identifiers such as ISBN do not cover, but each library has its own scheme, so the numbers are unique only within a country.
tldr.mechanism: A URN namespace named NBN builds each name from an ISO country code, optional sub-namespace codes, a hyphen and the locally assigned NBN string, so URN:NBN names are globally unique.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8458 replaces RFC 3188 with a revised registration (version 4) that follows RFC 8141, drops unused features and updates the resolution guidance.

facts.label: Prefix
facts.value: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code, plus optional sub-namespaces

facts.label: Delimiters
facts.value: Colon within the prefix, hyphen before the NBN string

today: RFC 8458 obsoletes RFC 3188 and is an Informational RFC. The unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it, so it holds the current NBN namespace registration.

sections.title: NBNs and the URN:NBN Namespace
sections.content:
National Bibliography Numbers (NBNs) are identifiers that national libraries and partner organizations use for resources in their collections. They are usually applied to things that established systems such as ISBN do not cover, though they can also label component resources, for example JPEG images of the pages of a digitized book that has an ISBN.

Unlike ISBN or ISSN, NBN is not one identifier system with a standard scope and syntax. Each implementer creates its own system with its own assignment rules. The RFC records that URN:NBNs are in production use in several European countries, including Austria, Finland, Germany, Hungary, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland, and have been applied to Web archives, digitized materials, research data and doctoral dissertations.

The first NBN namespace was specified in 2001 in RFC 3188. This document replaces it and fits the namespace into the revised URN framework of RFC 8141.
sections.eli5: Libraries number the things they keep, but each country numbers them its own way. This document explains how to turn those numbers into names that work on the internet.

sections.title: Assigning URN:NBNs
sections.content:
Assignment is controlled at the national level by the national library, or libraries if there is more than one. A library may let trusted partners such as universities or government institutions assign NBNs within a sub-namespace, and the partner may divide it further. If several libraries share a country, they MUST agree how to split the national namespace before assignment begins.

NBNs are unique only nationally, so when used as URNs they MUST be augmented with a prefix based on the nation's ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code. This is what makes URN:NBNs globally unique. Once assigned, an NBN MUST be persistent, a URN:NBN MUST NOT be reused for another resource, and users MUST ensure that they never assign the same URN:NBN twice. The RFC suggests assigning sequentially by program, or using printable checksums such as SHA-1 as NBNs.
sections.eli5: Every country library hands out its own numbers and adds its country letters in front, like a phone number with a country code. Once a number is given out, it is never given to anything else.

sections.title: Syntax and Equivalence
sections.content:
The namespace-specific string has three parts: a prefix made of the country code and optional sub-namespace codes separated by colons, a hyphen, and an NBN string assigned by the library or its delegate. Examples from the RFC are urn:nbn:fi-fe201003181510, urn:nbn:ch:bel-9039 and urn:nbn:se:uu:diva-3475.

The whole prefix is case insensitive, but NBN strings may be case sensitive at the assigning authority's preference, so parsers MUST treat them as case sensitive. Sub-namespace identifiers MUST be registered at the national level, are case insensitive, and MUST NOT contain colons or hyphens. Non-ASCII characters MUST be translated into the canonical form specified in RFC 8141.

Two URN:NBNs are lexically equivalent if they are octet-by-octet equal after converting the leading urn:nbn: token, the prefix and any percent-encoded characters to a single case. Resolvers do not currently support the r-component or q-component. The f-component can be used if the resource's media type supports it, and the namespace adds no restrictions of its own.
sections.eli5: A name looks like country, then maybe a department, then a dash, then the library's own number. Capital letters in the country part do not matter, but they might in the number.

sections.title: Resolution and Persistence
sections.content:
Eventually URNs might be resolved through a Global Resolver Discovery Service (GRDS), with the country prefix as the hint for finding the right resolver. Because no GRDS has been installed yet, URN:NBNs are embedded in HTTP URIs whose authority part points to the right national resolver. The RFC's example is Finland, where the resolver is http://urn.fi, giving http://urn.fi/URN:NBN:fi-fe201003181510.

The RFC discusses three kinds of persistence: of the object, of the identifier and of the resolver. Digital resources need frequent migration, and a lifetime over 10 to 20 years can be considered long, but libraries commonly keep earlier versions as well. Persistent identifiers let a library link all versions of a resource, so a user can pick the original or the latest. If a version has disappeared, resolution can supply a surrogate, such as a metadata record or a newer digital version.
sections.eli5: Because there is no worldwide phone book for these names yet, you put the name after the web address of your country's library, and that library looks it up for you.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document only defines how to encode NBNs as URNs. Resolution is described at a generic level, so secure or authenticated resolution and user authentication are out of scope. No global validation mechanism is specified beyond checking characters that need special encoding in URIs.

An authority can nevertheless give its NBNs a rich syntax, such as fixed length and a checksum, which makes it possible to validate them programmatically. Intellectual property rights for the identified objects, and rights to the databases behind resolution services, are also out of scope. No specific security threats have been identified beyond those in the underlying documents.
sections.eli5: This document only says how to write the names. It does not promise anything about who is allowed to look them up or whether the lookups are safe.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3188
sections.content:
The revision is the namespace registration version 4, dated 2018-04-09, and is built on the new URN syntax of RFC 8141. The main differences from RFC 3188 are:

  • NBNs that are not based on ISO 3166 country codes are removed, due to lack of usage.
  • The whole NBN prefix is now declared case insensitive, in accordance with established practice.
  • Use of query and fragment components is specified in accordance with RFC 8141.
  • Numerous clarifications have been made based on a decade of experience, and the sections on resolution have been updated.

IANA has updated the existing registration of the NBN namespace using the template in the document.
sections.eli5: After ten years of use, the rules were tidied up. Rarely used options were dropped, and the rules were fitted to the newer web-name standard.

data.title: ABNF for the namespace-specific string
data.code:
nbn-nss     = prefix "-" nbn-string
prefix      = iso-cc *( ":" subspc )
            ; The entire prefix is case insensitive.
iso-cc      = 2ALPHA
            ; Alpha-2 country code as assigned by part 1 of ISO 3166
subspc      = 1*(ALPHA / DIGIT)
            ; As assigned by the respective national library.
nbn-string  = path-rootless
            ; The "path-rootless" rule is defined in RFC 3986.
